Cheat Sheet#

Theory#

Pipeline steps#

Indexing (offline) Query (online)
Upload → validate (type, size ≤ 20 MB, SHA-256) → store original → queue Auth (verified groups) → cache lookup → rewrite / self-query / route
Extract (route: text → OCR → VLM) → clean (NFKC, headers, hyphens, ₹) Hybrid: vector + BM25 with filters (ACL, status, model)
Redact PII → chunk (structure-aware, heading path) → scan injection Fuse with RRF (k = 60) → rerank 25–100 → keep 3–10
Embed (store model name) → replace chunks in one transaction → indexed Similarity threshold → prompt (edges order, token budget) → LLM → check citations/guardrails → stream

Decision rules#

Use… When…
RAG Shared facts that change often
API tool (user token) Live personal data ("my order")
Prompting first, then fine-tuning Style/behaviour
Text-to-SQL Aggregations ("average", "how many")
Agentic RAG Multi-part/comparison questions (cap steps)
GraphRAG "How are X and Y related?" — only if plain RAG fails
Hybrid search Always in production; essential for codes, IDs, and SKUs
Reranker On the short list; skip when the top result is far ahead
Multi-query / HyDE Only for failing question types / low top score
Exact search < ~100k vectors or very selective filter
HNSW / IVF / PQ Speed+recall (RAM) / fast build, less memory / tiny memory + re-score
pgvector Already on Postgres with ≤ tens of millions of chunks
Multilingual embeddings Any Hindi, Hinglish, or other non-English users
Tesseract Clean typed scans, high volume
VLM / doc parser Complex layouts, tables, garbage OCR
Parent-child Need precise match + rich context
Fine-tune embeddings Rare domain terms after hybrid + rerank tried

Important numbers#

Thing Number
Golden set 50–200 Qs to start; ≥ 20% unanswerable; course has 33
Chunk size start ~200–400 tokens; bge-small max 512 input
Scanned page rule < 50 chars + has image → OCR
Retry back-off 10 s, 30 s, 60 s; capstone attempts reach 4
RRF k = 60
pgvector HNSW defaults m 16, ef_construction 64, ef_search 40
pgvector dims vector ≤ 2,000; halfvec ≤ 4,000
Filter trap ef_search 40 × 10% filter ≈ 4 rows
Candidates → final 30–100 → rerank → 3–10
Semantic cache threshold ≥ ~0.92
Context budget example ~1,500 tokens
Quantization memory fp16 ½, int8 ¼, binary 1/32
Common dims 384–1,024
Embedding cost 1M × 250-token chunks @ $0.02/1M ≈ $5
Batch APIs ~50% cheaper
Contextual retrieval gains −35% failures; −49% + BM25; −67% + rerank
Latency search 5–50 ms; rerank 50–300 ms; TTFT 0.3–2 s; full 1–10 s
Judge calibration human-grade 30–50 answers
DPDP rules 13 Nov 2025; main obligations May 2027

Key formulas#

  • RRF = Σ 1/(k + rank); MRR = 1 / rank of the first relevant result; precision@k = relevant results in top k ÷ k; recall@k = relevant results in top k ÷ all relevant results.
  • Unit vectors: ‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2·cos(a, b), which means cosine, dot product, and L2 all produce the exact same ranking.

Top pitfalls#

  1. Using different embedding models for docs vs. queries (or mixing models in one index).
  2. Silent extraction failures (scans contribute nothing).
  3. Creating chunks larger than the model input limit, which get silently truncated.
  4. Creating non-self-contained chunks without a heading path.
  5. Relying on vector-only search, which misses codes and IDs.
  6. Adding raw cosine and BM25 scores together.
  7. Falling into the post-filtering trap with selective filters or small tenants.
  8. Putting permissions in the prompt instead of the retrieval query, or trusting groups from the request body.
  9. Redacting PII only in the answer instead of at ingestion, or using a generic [PHONE] placeholder.
  10. Allowing free-form refusals or skipping the similarity threshold.
  11. Burying the best chunk in the middle, or sending too many chunks.
  12. Omitting unanswerable questions from the golden set, or looking only at averages without slicing.
  13. Using a same-provider LLM judge without human calibration.
  14. Leaving the semantic cache unscoped by permissions and index version.
  15. Promising sub-100 ms full answers or failing to stream responses.
  16. Re-indexing without idempotency, which causes duplicates or half-documents.
  17. Deleting old policy versions instead of archiving them.
21

Super Quick Revision#

Theory#

Read time: about 8 minutes. This page covers the whole unit in order. Each block is one idea you must be able to explain. Use the self-test at the end to check yourself.

In one line: Production RAG is two pipelines that meet at an index. Offline, messy documents become clean, permissioned chunks. Online, a question becomes a cited answer or an honest "I don't know". Security, evaluation and operations wrap both.

1. What RAG is and when to use it#

  • RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): find the most relevant pieces of your documents, put them in the prompt, and let the LLM answer only from them, with citations. It reduces hallucinations but does not remove them.
  • Why not just paste everything into a 1M-token context? Cost (you pay for every token on every question), latency (users expect first words in about 1 s), "lost in the middle", and long context cannot give you permissions, freshness or checkable citations.
  • Choose the right tool: Use RAG for facts in shared documents that change, an API call with the user's token for live personal data ("where is my order?"), text-to-SQL for aggregations ("how many", "average"), prompting then fine-tuning for tone and style, and an agent for multi-part questions.
  • Six qualities of production RAG: correct, honest, safe, fresh, fast and affordable, observable.

2. Offline: getting documents into the index#

  • Services, not a script. The Upload API checks file type and size, computes a SHA-256 hash to deduplicate, stores the original file, and pushes a job to a queue (Redis + RQ) for background workers. The upload returns at once; ingestion scales for throughput while queries scale for latency.
  • Never fail silently. Every document tracks a status. Temporary errors are retried with exponential back-off, while permanent errors go to a dead-letter queue with a failed status and a clear message—never retry forever.
  • Idempotency (running twice produces the same result as running once): combine a content hash, deterministic chunk IDs, and replacing old chunks in one transaction.
  • Keep the original file. The index holds only derived data, so you can rebuild from originals whenever OCR, chunking, or the embedding model improves.
  • Extraction sets the ceiling, and it fails silently. Route each page appropriately: use the text layer when present, fall back to OCR when a page has fewer than 50 characters and an image, and reserve VLMs for hard blocks. Tesseract is fine for clean typed scans. Clean the extracted text (NFKC normalization, repeated headers/footers, hyphenation, currency to ₹), write CSV rows with column names, and send aggregations to SQL.

3. Chunking and embeddings#

  • The chunk is the unit of everything: you embed, find, read, and cite chunks. A good chunk is coherent, self-contained, right-sized, and traceable.
  • Default recipe: create structure-aware chunks of ~200–400 tokens with the heading path prepended, and keep tables whole with their header row. Stay under the embedding model's input limit (bge-small reads 512 tokens and silently cuts off the rest).
  • When the default fails: use parent-child chunking (search small chunks, return the larger parent) for a precise match with rich context. Contextual chunks prepend a situating sentence, which drops retrieval failures by 35% (49% with BM25 and 67% with reranking).
  • Metadata on every chunk: store doc id, section, page, version, effective date, status, access groups, language, trust level, and embedding model. These power filters, permissions, citations, and updates.
  • An embedding is a vector of meaning where similar meanings point in similar directions. Use the same model for documents and questions, and store the model name with every vector. Use a multilingual model for Hindi or Hinglish users, and pick the model with your golden set rather than a public leaderboard.
  • On normalised vectors, cosine, dot product, and L2 give the same ranking. Matryoshka embeddings let you keep only the first dimensions, and int8 quantization uses ¼ of the memory while keeping almost all the quality.

4. Online: from question to retrieved chunks#

  • The funnel: apply filters, run hybrid search (30–100 candidates), rerank, keep 3–10 chunks, and build the prompt. Run cheap, broad steps first and slow, precise steps last.
  • Hybrid search: BM25 catches codes, IDs, SKUs, and rare words, while vectors catch paraphrases. Fuse them with RRF = Σ 1/(60 + rank); never add raw cosine and BM25 scores directly.
  • ANN indexes: HNSW is fast with high recall but uses more RAM; IVF builds faster with less memory; PQ uses tiny memory and re-scores with full vectors. In pgvector you must create the index yourself, and ef_search defaults to 40.
  • The filtering trap: ANN filters after searching, so a selective filter returns too few rows (40 × 10% ≈ 4). Fix it with iterative scan, a filter-aware engine, a per-tenant partition, or exact search.
  • Query work: always rewrite chat follow-ups. Self-query pulls filters out of the question, but it must never remove permission filters. Use multi-query or HyDE only for question types that fail, and route order questions to an API.
  • A reranker is a cross-encoder that reads the query and chunk together, so it catches details that embeddings miss. Run it only on the short list—it is often the cheapest big win.

5. Grounded generation#

  • Prompt rules: Answer only from the sources, cite [S#], use one exact refusal sentence, treat sources as data rather than instructions, prefer active and newest versions while mentioning conflicts, and answer in the user's language.
  • Wrap sources in XML tags that carry metadata (title, page, status, trust). Your code then checks that every [S#] exists, catches the refusal, and blocks secrets and banned promises.
  • Refuse in two layers: (1) before the LLM, when the best similarity is below a threshold (cheap); (2) inside the LLM, when the text is related but holds no answer.
  • Context: budget by tokens (about 1,500) instead of chunk count. Put the best chunk first and the second best last ("lost in the middle"). Filter out archived versions by default.

6. Security and privacy#

  • Permissions are a WHERE clause in retrieval, built from groups in the verified token. Never put permissions in the prompt, never take groups from the request body, and never let the LLM set them. If text is in the context, assume it can leak.
  • Redact PII at ingestion, before chunking and embedding: phone, PAN, Aadhaar (Verhoeff checksum), card (Luhn checksum), email. Use placeholders like [PII_PHONE], not [PHONE]. Use NER (Presidio) for names.
  • Indirect prompt injection hides inside retrieved documents (OWASP LLM01). Defend in layers: scan and flag at ingestion, use trust levels, fence sources, and guard the output. Also watch for data poisoning, embedding inversion and denial-of-wallet.

7. Evaluation#

  • Golden set: 50–200 questions covering every question type, with ≥ 20% unanswerable. Label documents and evidence strings, not chunk IDs, so labels survive re-chunking.
  • Measure retrieval and answers separately. Retrieval: hit@k, recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG. Answers: correctness, faithfulness, relevancy, refusal accuracy, citation validity.
  • Diagnose: If the right chunk is at rank 1 but the answer is wrong, generation failed; if the right chunk was never found, retrieval failed.
  • LLM judge: use a different provider from the generator, give it a rubric, and calibrate it on 30–50 human-graded answers. Change one thing at a time, gate every change in CI, and slice results by question type.

8. Operating in production#

  • Latency: retrieval takes tens of ms and the first token arrives in under 2 s. Stream the rest. Never promise whole answers in under 100 ms.
  • Caching: Use an exact cache, a semantic cache (≥ ~0.92, scoped by groups and index version), provider prompt caching (put fixed text first), and an embedding cache keyed by content hash and model.
  • Cost is mostly LLM tokens. Send fewer, better chunks, route easy questions to a cheap model, cache, cap output length, and use batch APIs (~50% cheaper) for offline work.
  • Observability: one trace per request with a span per stage. Alert on p95 latency, refusal rate, queue depth, and index size vs document count.
  • Freshness: re-ingest when the hash changes. On delete, remove the chunks and any cached answers. Archive old versions (don't delete them). Swap embedding models blue/green and check the golden set before cutover.
  • Graceful failure: If vector search is down, serve a keyword-only answer marked as degraded; if the LLM is down, retry and then fail over; if similarity is low, expand the query, refuse, and offer a human.

Quick self-test#

Question Answer
Docs embedded with model A, questions with model B. What happens? Results are basically random, because each model has its own vector space.
"What does E110 mean?" fails with vector search. Fix? Hybrid search: BM25 + vectors fused with RRF.
A customer retrieves salary bands. Where is the bug? Permissions are missing from the retrieval WHERE clause, or groups came from the request instead of the verified token.
Why use a fixed refusal sentence? Code can detect it, count it in metrics and route it to a human.
Filter on a 2% tenant returns zero rows. Why? The post-filtering trap: ANN searches first, then filters.
Where should PII be redacted? At ingestion, before chunking and embedding, never only in the answer.
Why must ≥ 20% of golden questions be unanswerable? Otherwise a system that always guesses scores as well as one that refuses correctly.
How do you change the embedding model with zero downtime? Blue/green: new column, backfill, build the index, shadow-evaluate on the golden set, then cut over.

If you remember only five things: (1) Garbage in, garbage retrieved: check extraction and chunking first. (2) Retrieval sets the ceiling for answer quality. (3) Permissions are a WHERE clause, not a prompt line. (4) "I don't know" is a feature; prove it with unanswerable questions. (5) Change one thing, then rerun the golden set.

Unit 2

Agentic RAG#

Build a CrewAI team that answers from your PDF, falls back to web search when the PDF has no answer, and grades its own work before replying.

22

Big Picture: End-to-End Architecture#

Theory#

About this course#

What this course is about: You will build a small AI team with CrewAI that answers questions from your own PDF, searches the internet when the PDF has no answer, and checks its own work before replying. You will learn plain RAG first and then build the agentic version file by file (config.py, llms.py, tools.py, agents.py, tasks.py, and main.py). The system uses DeepSeek as its brain, which you can run in the cloud through OpenRouter or locally on your laptop with Ollama.

The course uses a metro map analogy: a question enters at the Router junction and takes either the library line (our PDF) or the web line (the internet). Next, two inspectors (the graders) check the result, and if either check fails, a red fallback line reroutes it to web search.

Figure 14: Big Picture: End-to-End Architecture
FLOWCHART

Tip: The whole system has 5 agents, 5 tasks, 2 tools, and 2 LLMs. They run sequentially in one CrewAI Crew.

23

Why RAG exists#

Section 1

Theory#

In one line: A smart LLM that has never seen your documents is still guessing about them. RAG hands it the right pages at the moment it needs them.

Key concepts#

  • An LLM (Large Language Model), such as DeepSeek, is trained on huge amounts of public text, so it knows general topics like finance, Python, or Transformers.
  • However, it has never seen your private documents, such as internal reports, HR policies, contracts, or class notes.
  • If you ask about them, it says "I don't know" or, worse, confidently makes something up. This is called hallucination.
  • RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Read the words backwards to see how it works:
    • Generation: the LLM writes an answer,
    • Augmented: after we first add extra information to its prompt,
    • Retrieval: which we have fetched from our own documents.
  • No retraining or fine-tuning is needed: we simply add the right text to the prompt.
  • Analogy: Think of it as an open-book exam—the student (the LLM) already knows the subject, but performs much better with the textbook open to the right page.

Why not paste the whole document into the prompt?#

  • A PDF can be hundreds of pages long, making it slow and costly to send in full—and often larger than the model's context window.
  • Instead, RAG sends only the few most useful pieces.
24

Traditional RAG, step by step#

Section 2

Theory#

In one line: There are two phases. Index the library once, then retrieve and generate for every question.

Figure 15: Traditional RAG, step by step
FLOWCHART

Step 1 — Load#

  • Read the source documents, such as PDFs, Word files, web pages, or text files.
  • This project uses one PDF: Attention Is All You Need, the research paper that introduced the Transformer (the "T" in GPT).

Step 2 — Split into chunks#

  • A chunk is a small piece of text, typically around 1,000–2,000 characters long.
  • Splitting text into small pieces lets us retrieve only the parts that matter.
  • Overlap: neighbouring chunks often share a little text, so a sentence cut at the edge is not lost.
  • Trade-off: smaller chunks are more precise but carry less context. Bigger chunks carry more context but also more noise.

Step 3 — Embed (text → numbers)#

  • An embedding model turns each chunk into a list of numbers called a vector.
  • The model used here is BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5. It produces 384 numbers per chunk.
  • Key property: Texts with similar meanings receive similar vectors, even when they use different words (for example, "How do I cancel my order?" and "Steps to stop a purchase" map close together).
  • Semantic search means searching by meaning, not by exact words.

Step 4 — Store in a vector database#

  • A vector database stores each vector plus its original text. It is built to find the most similar vectors fast.
  • This project uses ChromaDB. It runs on your laptop and saves to disk, so indexing happens only once.

Then, for every question#

  1. Embed the question with the same embedding model.
  2. Ask the vector database for the top-k most similar chunks (in our code, k is set to 4).
  3. Put the question and the chunks into a prompt and send it to the LLM.
  4. The LLM writes the answer.

Tip (rule you must not break): Embed the question and the documents with the same embedding model. Different models make different "maps", so distances between them mean nothing.

Tip: In the agentic version, this whole pipeline is wrapped inside one tool (rag_tool).

25

Where plain RAG struggles#

Section 3

Theory#

In one line: Plain RAG follows the same fixed path every time, even when that path is wrong.

Problem What happens
Retrieval can miss The top-k chunks are only loosely related, so the LLM answers from the wrong material.
Always searches the documents A question like "What's the weather today?" still digs through the PDF and produces a bad answer.
Can still hallucinate RAG reduces made-up facts a lot, but the LLM can still add facts that are not in the chunks.
Nobody checks the work The generated output goes straight to the user without any verification.
  • Analogy: Plain RAG is like a bus on a single fixed route, whereas Agentic RAG is a metro network where a smart station controller (the Router) picks the right line and inspectors (the Graders) check the train before it reaches the final station.
Figure 16: Where plain RAG struggles
FLOWCHART
26

Agentic RAG: the big idea#

Section 4

Theory#

In one line: Agentic RAG replaces the fixed pipeline with a small team of AI agents that decide, fetch, and double-check.

What is an agent?#

  • An agent is an LLM given a role, a goal, and permission to use tools.
  • The work is split across five specialists. Each one does one narrow job.
# Agent One job Real-life twin Output
1 Router Decides where the answer lives: the PDF or the internet Hospital reception desk vectorstore or websearch
2 Retriever Calls the tool the Router picked and brings back the information Librarian Retrieved answer + evidence
3 Answer Grader Checks whether the answer addresses the question (filters out wrong retrievals) Teacher: "did you answer what was asked?" yes / no
4 Hallucination Grader Checks whether every claim is supported by the source text Auditor: "show me the receipt" yes (grounded) / no
5 Answer Generator If both checks pass, polishes the answer; if either fails, searches the web and answers from those results News anchor Final answer

Two tools#

  • RAG tool: This wraps the whole traditional RAG pipeline from Section 2 into a single function.
  • Web search tool: This searches the internet and returns the top 3 results.
  • Tools are just functions, so you can easily add more later—such as a SQL DB, a graph DB for customer relationships, a calculator, or a company API. This makes the design powerful and easy to extend.

Two LLMs#

  • Main LLM: DeepSeek via OpenRouter serves as the brain of all five agents and orchestrates the workflow.
  • RAG LLM: A fast model on Groq lives inside the RAG tool and turns the retrieved chunks into a short answer, because speed matters here.
Figure 17: Agentic RAG: the big idea — Two LLMs
FLOWCHART

Tip (key shift): In plain RAG, the path is hard-coded. In agentic RAG, an LLM decides the path at run time and other LLMs verify the result. You trade some speed and cost for better routing and fewer wrong answers.

27

Follow one question, end to end#

Section 5

Theory#

In one line: It works like a relay race. Each agent does one lap and passes the baton.

Library line: "What is self-attention?"#

Figure 18: Follow one question, end to end — Library line: "What is self-attention?"
SEQUENCE
  • The Router receives the question along with a one-line note about what the PDF holds. It chooses vectorstore because self-attention is a Transformer topic.
  • The Retriever calls rag_tool("What is self-attention?") and returns SOURCE: document, the answer, and the 4 chunks used.
  • The Answer Grader returns yes because the answer addresses self-attention.
  • The Hallucination Grader receives the answer, the 4 chunks, and the relevance grade, then returns yes because every sentence traces back to a chunk.
  • The Answer Generator receives the answer and both grades, and produces a clean final answer with no mention of routing or grading.

Web line: "Who won yesterday's cricket match?"#

  • The Router chooses websearch, because a research paper cannot know yesterday's score.
  • The Retriever calls web_search_tool, which returns SOURCE: web and the top 3 results with titles, links, and text.
  • Both graders pass, so the Answer Generator writes a short answer based on the search results.

Failure line: the PDF answer contains a made-up fact#

  • The Router chooses vectorstore and the Retriever fetches good chunks, but the RAG answer adds a date that is not in them.
  • Answer Grader: returns yes because the answer is on topic.
  • Hallucination Grader: returns no because the date is not present in the source chunks.
  • The Answer Generator sees a "no" and does not trust the answer, so it runs a fresh web search and builds the final answer from the web results.

What one question costs#

Plain RAG Agentic RAG
LLM calls 1 About 7–8
Time A few seconds ~15 s to a few minutes, depending on model and provider
Money (DeepSeek V4 Flash) Practically zero Well under ₹1 per question
Live questions? No Yes, through web search
Self-checks? No Yes, twice
28

Real-world use cases#

Section 6

Theory#

In one line: The pattern is the same everywhere: private docs go on the library line, live data goes on the web/live line, and checks are added whenever mistakes are costly.

Use case Library line (docs) Live line (web/tool) Why checks matter Example question
Bank support Loan, FD, and credit-card policies; fee schedules Repo rate news and current offers (via web or bank API) A wrong foreclosure charge leads to complaints and penalties What is the penalty for closing an FD after 8 months?
Hospital help desk Visiting rules, admission checklist, and insurance/cashless docs Doctor availability (via appointment system tool) A made-up fasting instruction can harm a patient What documents are needed for cashless admission?

Plain RAG or agentic RAG?#

Figure 19: Real-world use cases — Plain RAG or agentic RAG?
FLOWCHART

Tip: Start simple. Many teams build plain RAG first, measure where it fails, and only then add a router or graders for those failures.

29

The toolbox we use#

Section 7

Theory#

Name What it is Our use
CrewAI Python framework for teams of AI agents ("crews") Agents, tasks, tools, running the team
DeepSeek An open LLM family from a Chinese AI lab that is affordable and strong at reasoning and agent work Serves as the main brain: DeepSeek V4 Flash in the cloud and DeepSeek-R1 on a laptop
OpenRouter One API key for hundreds of models from many providers (like a recharge that works on every network) Calling DeepSeek in the cloud
Groq A cloud provider running models on its own LPU chips, built for very fast inference Fast LLM inside the RAG tool
Ollama A free app to download and run LLMs locally Optional: runs DeepSeek fully locally
Tavily A search API made for AI agents that returns clean text instead of messy web pages Web search tool
ChromaDB Lightweight local vector database Storing the PDF's vectors
  • Inference means running a trained model to get an answer.

Tip (settings beat hard-coding): Providers add and retire models often. Groq stopped serving DeepSeek models in October 2025, which is why the RAG tool uses a fast Groq-hosted model (not DeepSeek). At the time of writing, OpenRouter had no free DeepSeek model, so the default is a cheap paid one. Every model name lives in .env, so you can swap a model without code changes.

30

Agent, Task, Tool, Crew#

Section 8

Theory#

In one line: Learn four words and any CrewAI project becomes readable.

Term Office analogy Answers
Agent An employee Who
Task An item on their to-do list What
Tool Equipment they may use (phone, library card) With what
Crew The whole team plus the work order How it runs
Figure 20: Agent, Task, Tool, Crew
FLOWCHART

Agent settings#

  • role: defines the job title, e.g. "Router".
  • goal: defines what success means, e.g. "Route user questions to the vectorstore or web search."
  • backstory: describes who the agent is and how it thinks ("You are an expert at deciding…"), addressing it like a person with expertise.
  • Other key settings include llm (its brain), allow_delegation (whether it may hand work to another agent—set to no here), and verbose (whether to print its thinking).

Task settings#

  • description: provides the instructions, including a {question} placeholder.
  • expected_output: specifies the exact shape of the result, e.g. "one word: yes or no".
  • agent: assigns who performs the task.
  • context: lists which earlier tasks' outputs it may read, which is how information flows down the line.

Prompt engineering is the real work#

Backstories and descriptions are prompts. Getting them right takes several rounds of trial and error. These three fixes came from real testing:

Problem seen Fix added to prompt
Router matched keywords instead of meaning "make routing decisions based on the semantic meaning of the question, not just keyword matching"
Graders wrote long explanations that confused the next agent "exactly one word: yes or no, no explanation"
Final answer explained how it was found "the final answer contains only the answer, not how you found it"

Tip: When an agent misbehaves, don't rewrite code first. Read its output in the terminal, then tighten its backstory, description, or expected_output.

31

Set up the project#

Section 9

Theory#

Step 0 — feel the flow (no keys)#


cd code
python step0_simulate_flow.py
  • This script shows the same 5 steps. In the demo, the Hallucination Grader catches a made-up fact: when asked "What is multi-head attention?", it flags the answer as not grounded (no), so the Answer Generator falls back to a web result.

Choose the brain (LLM_MODE)#

LLM_MODE What runs Cost Speed Best for
openrouter (default) DeepSeek V4 Flash, cloud Pay-as-you-go; a small credit lasts a long time Good Learning the real DeepSeek setup
groq Fast open model on Groq (not DeepSeek) Free tier Very fast Practice with zero payment
ollama DeepSeek-R1 8B on your laptop Free Slow on normal laptops Privacy and offline learning

.env#

  • Copy .env.example to a file named exactly .env, then paste your keys after = with no quotes and no spaces.

Tip (security): Never share or upload .env. Anyone with your keys can spend your credits. Add .env to .gitignore.

32

Plain RAG first#

Section 10

Theory#

In one line: First, see what one person working alone can and can't do: step1_plain_rag.py searches the PDF, makes one LLM call, and prints the result.


def plain_rag(question):
    library = create_pdf_search_tool(config.PDF_PATH)   # 1. indexing (slow only the first time)
    chunks = library.run(query=question)                # 2. retrieval: top-k chunks
    llm = get_rag_llm()                                 # 3. generation: one LLM call
    return clean_text(llm.call(RAG_PROMPT.format(context=chunks, question=question)))
  • One LLM call, so it is fast and cheap. There is no router, no web, no checks.

python step1_plain_rag.py "What is multi-head attention?"       # good answer
python step1_plain_rag.py "What is the weather in Delhi today?" # NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT
  • For the weather question, the best plain RAG can do is NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT. It has nowhere else to look.
33

config.py and llms.py#

Section 11

Theory#

In one line: config.py is the one place for settings. llms.py is the one place for the two brains.

config.py#

  • LLM_MODE is a three-way switch (openrouter, groq, or ollama). Running Ollama locally needs ~8 GB of free RAM.
  • RAG_LLM_MODE can be set to groq (fast cloud) or same (reuse the main brain, with no Groq key needed).
  • The main model must support tools (function calling), because the Retriever calls tools and not every model can—check openrouter.ai/models.
  • PDF_TOPIC is a one-line description of the PDF's contents. The Router never opens the PDF; instead, it decides from this line plus the question, so update it if you use your own PDF.
  • Safety limits:
Setting Default Meaning
WEB_RESULTS 3 Web results to fetch
TOP_K 4 PDF chunks to retrieve
MAX_RPM 10 Max LLM calls per minute (since free tiers are strict), acting like a speed governor on a school bus

llms.py#

  • LLM(...) is CrewAI's universal model connector, like a universal charger with different tips. The prefix before the first slash picks the provider: openrouter/…, ollama/…, openai/….
  • temperature=0.1 (main) keeps answers calm and consistent. Higher values are more creative, which is bad for routing and grading; the Groq LLM uses temperature=0.0.
  • @lru_cache(maxsize=1) means build once and reuse, so all five agents share one brain object.
  • clean_text() strips <think>…</think> blocks. Reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 write private "rough work" there. We keep only the final answer.
34

tools.py#

Section 12

Theory#

In one line: These are the hands of the agents. One searches our PDF, and one searches the web.

create_pdf_search_tool — the library#

  • Uses CrewAI's PDFSearchTool, which handles the whole indexing phase: loading, chunking, embedding, and storing in ChromaDB.
  • collection_name acts as the "shelf". It is named <pdf stem>_<embedding model name>, with special characters replaced by _ and truncated to 60 chars, so switching the PDF or the model never mixes old and new vectors.
  • The embedding provider "sentence-transformer" runs locally, downloading the model once from Hugging Face (~130 MB).

create_rag_tool — retrieval + fast generation#

Figure 21: tools.py — create_rag_tool — retrieval + fast generation
FLOWCHART
  • @tool("rag_tool") turns the function into something an agent can call.
  • The docstring is an instruction, not decoration. The agent learns what the tool does from its name and docstring.
  • RAG_PROMPT rules: "Use ONLY the context, with no outside knowledge. If the answer isn't there, reply with exactly NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT. Answer in 3 to 6 clear sentences."
  • It returns both the answer and the chunks. The chunks are the evidence the Hallucination Grader needs, like receipts attached to an expense claim.

web_search_tool#

  • Calls TavilyClient(api_key).search(query=question, max_results=3).
  • It is wrapped in try/except so that on failure (no internet, wrong key, or limit reached), it returns WEB_SEARCH_FAILED: <error> instead of crashing the crew—because one broken tool shouldn't stop the whole office.

Common mistake (real bug): The web tool failed with "missing 1 required positional argument" because the agent called it without the question. The fix had two parts: the tool docstring says "Input must be the user's full question", and the task descriptions say "pass it the question: '{question}'". When an agent calls a tool wrongly, fix the instructions it reads.

35

agents.py#

Section 13

Theory#

In one line: Five job descriptions with the same structure and a different personality.

All agents share these settings: allow_delegation=False, max_iter=5, verbose=True, llm=get_main_llm().

Agent Goal (short) Key backstory points
Router Route to the vectorstore (PDF) or the web based on what the question is really about Told what the DB contains via PDF_TOPIC, and decides by semantic meaning rather than keywords
Retriever Use the tool the router chose to fetch info Calls exactly the tool it is told to, passes the full question, and never adds facts that are not in the context
Answer Grader Filter out wrong or irrelevant retrievals Strict grader that judges one thing: does it address the question? If key ideas are present, it counts as relevant
Hallucination Grader Catch made-up facts before they reach the user Fact checker that verifies whether every important claim is supported by the source; invented facts, numbers, or names count as hallucination
Answer Generator Produce one clear, correct, concise final answer Final editor that polishes the answer if checks pass, or runs a fresh web search if they fail; never explains its internal process
  • max_iter=5: allows at most 5 think-and-act rounds before the agent must answer, acting as a safety brake that stops endless loops from burning credits.

Tip: Tools are attached to tasks, not agents in this design. That way the same agent can be reused for other tasks with different tools.

36

tasks.py#

Section 14

Theory#

In one line: This is the to-do list, plus the wiring (context) that passes each result to the next agent.

Figure 22: tasks.py
FLOWCHART

Solid arrows show the run order. Dashed arrows show extra context a task may read.

Task Agent context tools expected_output
1. route Router — — Exactly one word: vectorstore or websearch. No explanation or punctuation
2. retrieve Retriever [router_task] [rag_tool, web_search_tool] First line SOURCE: document or SOURCE: web, then the answer, then the supporting text copied as is
3. grade Answer Grader [retriever_task] — One word: yes (relevant) / no
4. hallucination Hallucination Grader [retriever_task, grader_task] — One word: yes (grounded, no hallucination) / no
5. answer Answer Generator [retriever_task, grader_task, hallucination_task] [web_search_tool] Clear, concise answer in plain language (~3–6 sentences)

Key rules inside the descriptions#

  • '{question}' is a placeholder that crew.kickoff(inputs={"question": ...}) fills in everywhere.
  • Router rules: If the question's topic is covered by the document (even with different words), choose vectorstore. If it asks for current or real-time info (news, prices, scores, today's events) or a general topic not in the doc, choose websearch.
  • Retriever rules: Use rag_tool for vectorstore and web_search_tool for websearch. If rag_tool returns NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT, it falls back to the web with the same question. Always pass the full question.
  • Answer rules: If both grades are yes, polish the retrieved answer; if either is no, call web_search_tool and answer from those results. The final answer contains only the answer, not how it was found.
  • context=[router_task] lets the retriever read the router's output. It does not re-run the router or share its tools.

Tip: Relevance is not the same as grounding. An answer can be on-topic but invented, or true but off-topic, which is why both checks exist.

Common mistake: For the Hallucination task, "yes" means SAFE (grounded). It does not mean "yes, there is a hallucination".

37

main.py#

Section 15

Theory#

In one line: main.py has no intelligence. It just builds the team and presses start.

build_crew()#

  1. Tools: Calls create_rag_tool(PDF_PATH), which triggers indexing on the first run only; later runs reuse the vector DB.
  2. Crew: Builds Crew(agents=[...], tasks=[...], process=Process.sequential, max_rpm=config.MAX_RPM, verbose=True).
  • Process.sequential: runs tasks one after another in list order, making it simple and easy to debug.
  • max_rpm: allows at most 10 LLM calls per minute for the whole team; if they go faster, CrewAI waits.

ask() and main()#

  • crew.kickoff(inputs={"question": question}) starts the team.
  • After the run, every task's output is still available. The code reads the one-word results of the Router and both graders to print a journey line: route=… relevant=… grounded=… time=…s (like a train ticket listing the stations).
  • config.check_keys() runs before anything expensive and prints "Please fix your .env file first".
  • --chat mode keeps the team ready for question after question. The PDF is indexed only once. Type exit or quit (or press Enter on an empty line) to stop.
38

Run it and read the output#

Section 16

Theory#

In one line: Ask one question the PDF can answer and one it can't, then read the agent-by-agent output.


python main.py
python main.py "What is multi-head attention?"
python main.py "What is the latest stable version of Python?"
python main.py --chat

Why is it slow?#

  • The crew makes about 7–8 LLM calls per question across the 5 agents, a tool call, and the RAG LLM.
  • Fast providers take ~15–30 s. Free or overloaded models can take several minutes (one slow free model once took ~10 min). Ollama on a laptop also takes minutes.
39

Run DeepSeek on your laptop#

Section 17

Theory#

In one line: With Ollama you need no API key for the brain and get full privacy, but it is slower and less accurate on small hardware.


ollama pull deepseek-r1:8b      # ~5 GB download; needs ~8 GB free RAM

  • The brain then runs at http://localhost:11434. Only Tavily (web search) still needs the internet.

  • An 8B model on a normal laptop is for learning. Production local setups need a GPU.

Common mistake: Using the tiny 1.5B model. It downloads fast, but small models often fail to call tools in the right format, so the Retriever gets stuck (like a fresher who knows theory but can't fill in office forms). Use 8B or bigger.

40

When things break#

Section 18

Theory#

You see Why Fix
"Please fix your .env file first" A key is empty The file must be named .env (not .env.example) and sit in the code folder
404 / model not found The model ID no longer exists Find a current ID on the provider's models page. Update OPENROUTER_MODEL / GROQ_MODEL
429 / rate limit Too many requests on a free tier Wait, lower MAX_RPM, or use a paid model
WEB_SEARCH_FAILED No internet, wrong Tavily key, or limit reached Check key and connection. The rest of the team keeps working
Embedding dimension error The DB was built with a different embedding model The shelf name includes the model, so changing EMBEDDING_MODEL creates a fresh shelf. If you renamed things manually, use a new PDF_PATH name
41

Questions learners ask#

Section 19

Theory#

  • How does the Router know if the answer is in the PDF without reading it? It judges the question's meaning against PDF_TOPIC. It's an educated guess, not a lookup. The safety nets are the Retriever's fallback and the two graders. A stronger design gives the Router a quick "peek" tool to check the vector DB first.
  • Why a vector DB and not SQL? Text is split into tokens, and models represent meaning as long number lists. Large models use thousands of numbers per token; our embedding model uses 384 per chunk. SQL is great at exact matches ("find customer 42") but bad at "find the 4 rows whose 384 numbers are closest". A vector DB is built and indexed for similarity search.
  • How would I deploy this?
    • Simple start: Put the API on a cloud server such as AWS EC2, and add a GPU only if you self-host the LLM.
    • Many users: Run several copies behind a load balancer, plus a queue for long jobs since answers take seconds to minutes.
    • Models: APIs are fastest to ship, whereas self-hosting helps privacy and cost at scale but needs more maintenance.
  • Can I use it for company documents? Yes. Put the PDF in data/ and set PDF_PATH and a good PDF_TOPIC. For many docs, point the tool at a folder or build one library per department. Test with 20–30 real user questions and check the answers by hand. For confidential docs, use Ollama or a company-approved provider.
  • Why two LLMs? Different jobs need different strengths. The orchestrator needs reasoning. The RAG step is simple ("summarise these chunks") but sits mid-flow, so a very fast model keeps the run snappy.
42

Glossary#

Section 20

Theory#

Term Meaning
Tool calling (function calling) The LLM's ability to request "run this function with these inputs" in a structured format
Token A small piece of text (often part of a word). Pricing and limits are counted in tokens
43

Quick Mental Map#

Theory#

In one line: Agentic RAG is plain RAG plus decisions. A router picks the source, graders check the answer, and a fallback repairs failures. That is five agents, five tasks, two tools and two LLMs in one sequential crew.

Figure 23: Quick Mental Map — Agentic RAG
MIND MAP

The map in words#

Branch The question it answers Go deeper
Plain RAG base Can one retrieve-then-answer pass solve it? Traditional RAG · Plain RAG first
Route Where should this question look? Agentic RAG: the big idea · agents.py
Retrieve Which tool, and what happens when it finds nothing? tools.py
Grade Is the answer relevant and grounded? tasks.py
Generate Polish it or fall back? Follow one question, end to end
CrewAI blocks How do I wire the team together? Agent, Task, Tool, Crew · main.py
Brains Which model runs where? config.py and llms.py · Run DeepSeek on your laptop

Memory hooks#

  • The metro map: A question enters at the Router junction, takes either the library line or the web line, passes through two inspectors, and falls back to the web along the red fallback line if a check fails.
  • Hallucination grader "yes" means grounded, not "hallucinated".
  • Fix the prompt before the code: adjust the backstory, description, or expected_output first.
  • Agentic costs ~7–8 LLM calls vs 1. Pay that cost only when data is live or mistakes are costly.
44

Step-by-Step Guide for Similar Problems#

Theory#

In one line: Use this guide when a document Q&A system must also handle questions the documents cannot answer, and must check itself before replying.

Plain RAG, agentic RAG or deep search?#

If the problem looks like… Reach for…
All answers are in your docs; 1–2 s latency; cheap mistakes; ~zero budget Plain RAG (Unit 1)
Some answers need live or general web data Agentic RAG with a router and web fallback
Wrong answers are costly Add relevance and grounding graders
Multi-source, high-stakes research with conflicting facts Deep search (Unit 3)

The steps#

Step 1 — Start with plain RAG and a test set#

  • Do: Collect 20–30 real questions, including ones the document cannot answer. Build the plain pipeline: load the PDF, split it into chunks (1,000–2,000 chars with overlap), embed them with bge-small, store them in ChromaDB, retrieve top-k 4 chunks, and send them to the LLM.
  • Done when: you know exactly which questions plain RAG fails, and why.

Step 2 — Turn each failure type into a decision#

  • Do: Map each failure mode to a fix: use a router when the source is wrong (live or general info), a relevance grader for off-topic answers, a hallucination grader for invented details, and a fallback tool when nothing is found.
  • Decide: add only the decisions your failures justify, since each one costs extra LLM calls and seconds.

Step 3 — Define the tools#

  • Do: Give each tool one job using @tool("name") with a docstring that clearly states its inputs and outputs. The RAG tool should return a sentinel like NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT instead of guessing, while the web tool returns the top 3 results with URLs.
  • Done when: an agent can call each tool without "missing required argument" errors.

Step 4 — Design one agent per decision#

  • Do: Give each agent a role, goal, and backstory. The router knows PDF_TOPIC, graders must answer with one word, and the final generator gets the web tool for fallback.

Step 5 — Write the tasks and wire the context#

  • Do: Give each task a description and an expected_output, pass earlier results with context=[...], and use {question} placeholders filled by crew.kickoff(inputs=...).

Step 6 — Pick and pin the brains#

  • Do: Pair a main reasoning model (≥ 8B so tool calling works, temperature 0.1) with a fast, cheap RAG model (temperature 0.0). Share one instance with @lru_cache, choose the provider by model prefix, and keep keys in .env—never in git.

Step 7 — Assemble the crew with guard rails#

  • Do: Use Process.sequential, max_rpm (10), and max_iter (5) per agent, and run in verbose mode first.

Step 8 — Run, read the trace, tune#

  • Do: Run the test set, read every agent's output, and fix prompts before code. Track latency (~15–30 s) and LLM calls per question.
  • Done when: both grader paths (polish and fallback) are exercised and correct.

Step 9 — Choose how to deploy#

  • Decide: Use a hosted API for speed and easy setup, or self-host (on a GPU) for privacy or high volume, and plan for rate limits on free tiers.

Worked example: product-manual assistant that also knows "today"#

Step Applied to the new problem
1 Plain RAG over router manuals works for setup questions, but fails on "Is there a firmware update this week?"
2 That failure needs a router (manual vs live info) and a fallback; invented model numbers need a hallucination grader.
3 manual_search returns NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT; web_search is limited to the official support site.
4 PDF_TOPIC = "Acme home-router manuals", so release, price and outage questions route to the web.
8 Test set includes firmware, pricing and troubleshooting questions so every route is covered.

Red flags while approaching#

  • Jumping to agentic RAG before measuring where plain RAG fails.
  • Vague tool docstrings, which cause "missing required argument" errors.
  • Long grader explanations that confuse the next agent.
  • Tiny models (< 8B) that cannot call tools.
  • Forgetting to update PDF_TOPIC when the document changes.
  • Missing max_rpm or max_iter limits, which can trigger 429 rate-limit errors and infinite loops.

46

Cheat Sheet#

Theory#

The team at a glance#

Order Agent Reads (context) Tools Outputs
1 Router question + PDF_TOPIC — vectorstore / websearch
2 Retriever router rag_tool, web_search_tool SOURCE: … + answer + evidence
3 Answer Grader retriever — yes/no (relevant?)
4 Hallucination Grader retriever, grader — yes/no (yes = grounded)
5 Answer Generator retriever, grader, hallucination web_search_tool Final 3–6 sentence answer

Pipeline steps#

  • Indexing (once): Load the PDF, split it into chunks (1,000–2,000 chars with overlap), embed with bge-small (384-d), and store in ChromaDB.
  • Per question (plain): Embed the question with the same model, fetch the top-k (4) chunks, and send them to the LLM for an answer.
  • Per question (agentic): Route to the right source, retrieve the answer (falling back to the web if NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT), grade relevance, grade grounding, and then polish the answer—or run a web fallback if either grade is no.

Decision rules#

  • If the question is about a topic in the doc (even using different words), route to vectorstore.
  • If it asks for real-time info (news, prices, scores, today's events) or a general topic not in the doc, route to websearch.
  • If rag_tool returns NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT, retry on the web.
  • If both grades are yes, polish the answer; if either is no, run a fresh web search.
  • If all answers live in docs, you need 1–2 s latency, mistakes are cheap, and the budget is ~zero, use plain RAG. If you need live data, mistakes are costly, and you have budget for several calls, use agentic RAG.
  • Choose an API for speed and easy setup, or self-host (with a GPU in production) for privacy or high volume.
  • If you have no Groq key, set RAG_LLM_MODE=same; for free practice, use LLM_MODE=groq; for offline or private runs, use LLM_MODE=ollama.
  • When an agent misbehaves, fix the prompt (backstory, description, or expected_output) before touching the code.

Important numbers#

Item Value
Top-k (TOP_K) 4
Web results (WEB_RESULTS) 3
MAX_RPM 10
max_iter per agent 5
Embedding size 384 (bge-small-en-v1.5, ~130 MB)
Temperature 0.1 main, 0.0 Groq
LLM calls per question Plain 1; agentic ~7–8
Time per question ~15–30 s fast; minutes on free/local (~10 min worst seen)
Ollama model deepseek-r1:8b, ~5 GB, ~8 GB RAM, port 11434
Pre-launch test set 20–30 real questions

Defaults (.env)#

LLM_MODE=openrouter · OPENROUTER_MODEL=deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash · RAG_LLM_MODE=groq · GROQ_MODEL=llama-3.3-70b-versatile · EMBEDDING_MODEL=BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 · PDF_PATH=data/attention_is_all_you_need.pdf · PDF_URL=https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762

Commands#


python step0_simulate_flow.py                 # feel the flow, no keys
pip install -r requirements.txt
python step1_plain_rag.py "question"          # plain RAG
python main.py "question"                     # agentic RAG
python main.py --chat                         # chat mode (type exit to stop)
ollama pull deepseek-r1:8b                    # local brain

Key code idioms#

  • LLM(model="openrouter/…" | "ollama/…" | "openai/…"): the prefix picks the provider.
  • @lru_cache(maxsize=1) creates one shared brain, while @tool("name") plus a docstring defines an agent tool.
  • Task(..., context=[earlier_tasks], tools=[...]) · Crew(..., process=Process.sequential, max_rpm=10).
  • crew.kickoff(inputs={"question": q}) fills every {question}.

Pitfalls#

  • Using different embedding models for questions and docs produces meaningless distances.
  • Forgetting to update PDF_TOPIC for a new PDF causes wrong routing.
  • Reading the hallucination "yes" as "hallucinated"—it actually means grounded.
  • Vague tool docstrings cause "missing required argument" errors.
  • Long grader explanations confuse the next agent, so force one word.
  • Tiny models (1.5B) can't call tools reliably, so use ≥ 8B.
  • Committing .env leaks API keys and exposes your credits.
  • Free tiers hit 429 rate limits after a few questions, so lower MAX_RPM.
  • Expecting plain RAG to answer live questions won't work—it can only return NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT.
47

Super Quick Revision#

Theory#

Read time: about 6 minutes. This page covers the whole unit in order. Each block is one idea you must be able to explain. Use the self-test at the end to check yourself.

In one line: Agentic RAG is plain RAG plus decisions. A router picks the source, two graders check the answer, and a fallback repairs failures. That is 5 agents, 5 tasks, 2 tools and 2 LLMs in one sequential CrewAI crew.

1. Why RAG, and the plain RAG baseline#

  • An LLM has never seen your private documents, so it guesses or makes things up (hallucination). RAG is an open-book exam: it adds the right pages to the prompt, with no retraining or fine-tuning.
  • Indexing (once): Load the PDF, split it into chunks (1,000–2,000 characters with overlap), embed with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (384 numbers), and store them in ChromaDB on disk.
  • Per question: Embed the question with the same model, fetch the top-k = 4 chunks, and make one LLM call to generate the answer.
  • Where plain RAG struggles: retrieval can miss; it always searches the PDF even for "today's weather"; it can still hallucinate; and nobody checks the output. The best it can do for a live question is return NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT.

2. The agentic idea: the metro map#

  • An agent is an LLM with a role, a goal, and permission to use tools. In plain RAG the path is hard-coded, whereas in agentic RAG an LLM chooses the path at run time and other LLMs check the result.
  • The relay of five agents:
    1. Router chooses vectorstore or websearch by comparing the question's meaning against PDF_TOPIC (it never opens the PDF).
    2. Retriever calls the chosen tool; if rag_tool says NOT_FOUND_IN_DOCUMENT, it retries on the web.
    3. Answer Grader returns yes or no to indicate whether the answer addresses the question.
    4. Hallucination Grader returns yes or no to indicate whether every claim is supported by the source (yes = grounded = safe).
    5. Answer Generator polishes the answer if both grades are yes; if either is no, it runs a fresh web search and answers from those results. The final answer never explains how it was found.
  • Relevance ≠ grounding. An answer can be on topic but invented, or true but off topic. That is why there are two graders.

3. Two tools and two LLMs#

  • rag_tool wraps the whole plain RAG pipeline. It returns the answer and the chunks, because the chunks are the evidence (the "receipts") the Hallucination Grader needs.
  • web_search_tool calls Tavily and returns the top 3 results. On failure it returns WEB_SEARCH_FAILED: … instead of crashing the crew.
  • Main LLM: DeepSeek via OpenRouter, temperature 0.1. It runs all five agents and must support tool calling.
  • RAG LLM: a fast Groq model, temperature 0.0, inside the RAG tool. The orchestrator needs reasoning; the mid-flow summary step needs speed.
  • Tools are plain functions, so you can add more: SQL, a graph DB, a calculator, a company API.

4. CrewAI in four words#

  • Agent (who): role, goal, backstory, llm, allow_delegation=False, max_iter=5 (a safety brake against endless loops).
  • Task (what): description with a {question} placeholder, expected_output (e.g. "one word: yes or no"), agent, context, tools. In this design, tools are attached to tasks, not agents.
  • Tool (with what): @tool("name"). The docstring is an instruction, because the agent learns from it when and how to call the tool.
  • Crew (how it runs): Crew(agents, tasks, process=Process.sequential, max_rpm=10). crew.kickoff(inputs={"question": q}) fills every {question}.
  • context=[earlier_task] is how results flow down the line. It lets a task read an earlier output without re-running that task.

5. Prompt engineering is the real work#

  • Backstories, descriptions, and expected_output are prompts. Three fixes came from real testing: route by semantic meaning, not keywords; force graders to answer with exactly one word; and ensure the final answer contains only the answer.
  • Real bug: "missing 1 required positional argument". The agent called the web tool without the question. The fix was in the prompts, not the code: the docstring says "Input must be the user's full question" and the task says "pass it the question".
  • Rule: when an agent misbehaves, read its terminal output, then fix the prompt before touching the code.

6. Configuration, running and failures#

  • config.py holds every setting. LLM_MODE = openrouter (default) | groq (free practice) | ollama (private, offline). RAG_LLM_MODE = groq | same (when you have no Groq key). Keep model names in .env so you can swap models without code changes.
  • llms.py: the model prefix picks the provider (openrouter/…, ollama/…). @lru_cache(maxsize=1) means all agents share one brain. clean_text() strips <think>…</think> blocks.
  • The ChromaDB collection name includes the PDF name and the embedding model, so switching either never mixes old and new vectors.
  • Local brain: ollama pull deepseek-r1:8b (~5 GB, needs ~8 GB RAM). Don't use the 1.5B model, because tiny models can't call tools reliably.
  • Cost of agentic: ~7–8 LLM calls and ~15–30 s per question, vs 1 call for plain RAG. You pay this for live data and self-checks.
  • Common errors: "fix your .env" (wrong file name), 404 (model retired, so update the ID), 429 (rate limit, so lower MAX_RPM), WEB_SEARCH_FAILED (bad Tavily key or network issue), and embedding dimension errors (a DB built with another model). Never commit .env.

7. Plain RAG, agentic RAG or deep search?#

  • If all answers are in your docs, you need 1–2 s latency, mistakes are cheap, and the budget is ~zero, use plain RAG.
  • If some answers need live or general web data, add a router + web fallback; if wrong answers are costly, add graders.
  • For multi-source, high-stakes research with conflicting facts, use deep search (Unit 3).
  • Start simple. Build plain RAG and test it on 20–30 real questions. Then add only the decisions your measured failures justify, because each one costs calls and seconds.

Quick self-test#

Question Answer
How does the Router decide without reading the PDF? It judges the question's meaning against the one-line PDF_TOPIC. The fallback and the graders are the safety nets.
Hallucination Grader says "yes". Good or bad? Good: yes means the answer is grounded in the source.
What happens if either grade is "no"? The Answer Generator ignores that answer, runs a fresh web search and answers from the results.
Why does rag_tool return the chunks too? They are the evidence the Hallucination Grader checks claims against.
Why two LLMs? Reasoning for orchestration; raw speed for the simple summary step inside the tool.
What stops runaway loops and credit burn? max_iter=5 per agent and max_rpm=10 for the crew.
You switch to your own PDF. What must you update? PDF_PATH and PDF_TOPIC, or the Router will route wrongly.

If you remember only five things: (1) Follow the metro map: the Router sends questions to the library or web line, two inspectors check the result, and a red fallback line reroutes failures to the web. (2) Relevance and grounding are different checks. (3) A grader "yes" means grounded. (4) Fix the prompt before the code. (5) Agentic RAG costs ~7–8 calls instead of 1, so pay that cost only for live data or costly mistakes.

Unit 3

Deep Search Agents#

Multi-agent research that plans, searches in parallel, validates every source, merges evidence with provenance and repeats until the answer is good enough.

48

Big Picture: End-to-End Architecture#

Theory#

About this course#

Course by Shivank Agrawal (Future with Shivank), comprising 13 modules, 12 runnable labs, and a capstone (about 14–18 hours).

What this course is about: You will learn how to build a deep search agent, a multi-agent system that researches like a careful analyst. It plans the research, searches in parallel, checks every source for identity, authority, freshness, copies, and attacks, merges the evidence, and repeats until the answer is good enough—then shows where every claim came from. The running example is vendor due diligence on a fictional Indian payment gateway, NimbusPay.

The one idea to hold on to: Deep search is not "better search". It is a research workflow: plan → collect → validate → compare → merge → repeat until good enough → show your evidence.

Four layers and one loop. Every later module zooms into one box of the architecture, and the file names show where each component lives in the code pack (shivank-deep-search-agent/deepsearch/).

FLOWCHART
  • Orchestrator (orchestrator.py, class DeepSearchAgent) is the lead agent that runs this loop.
  • Each run writes its outputs to runs/<timestamp>-deepsearch/: report.md, report.json, evidence.json, and trace.jsonl.
