70

The Problem#

Section 1

Theory#

In one line: Security engineers spend 2–6 hours per vendor mostly finding and dating facts; the assessor handles the finding, dating, and checking, while leaving the judging to a person.

Why it matters#

  • Employees ask, "Can I use this AI tool?" several times a week.
  • Each request should trigger a vendor security review that answers typical questions such as:
    • Does the vendor hold a current SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certification? (See the Glossary for security certifications.)
    • Where is our data stored?
    • Do they train on our data?
    • Who are their sub-processors?
    • Have they had any security incidents?
    • Is a DPA (Data Processing Agreement) available?
  • The bottleneck today: Reviewers spend 2–6 hours per vendor reading trust centres, privacy policies, and news, so teams either wait weeks or skip the review altogether.

Running example: Nimbu Mart#

Its Information Security team has 8 internal documents (see the Data Pack).

The three fictional vendors#

Vendor What it does Why it's a good test
LedgerLens AI Summarises support tickets It has a solid SOC 2 Type II report, but stores data in the US/EU with India only "planned". It also tests several traps: a stale 2024 page, a same-name UK accountancy firm, a forum rumour, a review site contradicting the trust centre, and a blog with a prompt injection.
QuillDesk AI writing assistant It claims to be "SOC 2 compliant" with no report, trains on content by default, uses US-only storage, has a July 2026 incident with no post-mortem, and appears on a directory page that is a copy of the vendor's own page.
Parakeet Translate Translation for Indian languages This is the good vendor: it has ISO 27001 confirmed on the certifier's registry, an India region, no training on customer data, and a DPA with a DPDP addendum. However, it is approved only for internal data (T2), so customer-data use still needs Procurement.

What "good" looks like — LedgerLens at customer-data tier (abridged)#

Requirement Clause Verdict Why
Independent security assurance SEC-4.2 PASS SOC 2 Type II report dated 2026-01-20 (trust centre, 2026-09-01)
Customer data stored in India DP-3.1 FAIL India is only planned; today data is stored in the US and EU.
No training on our data AI-2.1 NEEDS REVIEW No training on Business/Enterprise tiers, whereas Free/Pro trains by default.
Sub-processors disclosed AI-3.4 NEEDS REVIEW A third-party model provider is present: Orbital Models (US).
Incident history SEC-9.3 NEEDS REVIEW One major incident occurred (2025-04) with a published post-mortem (2 sources).
On Approved Vendor List PROC-1.1 NEEDS REVIEW A review is already in progress; attach this assessment to it.

The report then contains:

  • Facts recorded with their confidence levels and conflicts.
  • A security section noting: "1 page quarantined for prompt injection; 1 rejected as a different company; 1 rumour dropped."
  • Six ready-to-send questions for the vendor.
  • An approval block with two required signers: Head of Information Security and DPO (Data Protection Officer).
  • Outcome: BLOCKED for this data tier — the system never outputs "rejected" or "approved".

Tip: Every row has a clause, verdict, reason, and evidence (source and date). If you can't fill in the evidence, the verdict must be UNKNOWN.

71

Architecture#

Section 2

Theory#

In one line: One graph handles three routes: policy questions stop at the graders, vendor-fact questions stop after research, and full assessments run the entire chain ending in a human decision.

Three routes#

Figure 39: Architecture — Three routes
FLOWCHART
  • The same nodes run as plain Python or as a LangGraph state machine (assessor/graph.py).
  • LangGraph is a library for building agent workflows as graphs of steps with shared state.

The components#

Component File Starter-kit status Your job
Contracts between stages assessor/schemas.py Complete. Defines 9 vendor fields, evidence levels, verdicts, and the report. —
Policy library assessor/policy_rag.py Simplified: uses clause chunking, BM25, ACL/version/trust filters, and extractive answers. Add hybrid search, reranking, and grounded generation.
Router assessor/router.py Rule-based mock Build an LLM router (using the course prompt plus 2 extra routes).
Graders assessor/graders.py Heuristic mocks Add two grader agents and a retry loop.
Vendor research assessor/vendor_research.py Includes a full offline loop (identity gate, quarantine, scoring, merging); live mode is a sequential baseline. Add a planner, parallel workers, memory, and live evaluation.
Requirement matcher assessor/matcher.py + data/requirements.yaml Complete & tested. Covers 8 rule types and 11 requirements. Extend it when adding new policies.
Questionnaire, report assessor/questionnaire.py, report.py Complete —
Guardrails assessor/guardrails.py Provides regex input redaction, an intent check, and an output policy. Add an LLM injection classifier and a red-team suite.
Orchestrator assessor/graph.py Runs in plain Python or LangGraph with the same nodes, plus a CLI human gate. Add a checkpointer with interrupt() and streaming.
API, UI app/api.py, app/ui.py Thin skeletons Add a queue, storage, auth, and a trace viewer.
Evaluation eval/run_eval.py, data/gold_set*.json The harness and fictional gold set are complete; the real-vendor set is a template. Fill it in.

Jargon:

  • BM25 is a classic keyword-ranking algorithm.
  • ACL stands for Access Control List, which defines who may see which document.
  • Extractive answer means copying the matching text directly, whereas grounded generation means the LLM writes an answer using only retrieved text, with citations.

Milestones (M0–M6)#

Section 3

Theory#

In one line: These seven milestones are completed in order, and each ends with a runnable "Done when" check.

Figure 40: Milestones (M0–M6)
FLOWCHART

M0 — Run and read the starter kit (½ day)#

Goal: Know exactly what the finished system does before changing anything.

  • Run the four demo questions in the README, then read each report.md and its trace.jsonl from bottom to top.
  • Open data/vendor_web/corpus.json to find the stale page, look-alike company, rumour, copy, and attack page. Predict what the system does, and check your prediction against the LedgerLens trace.
  • Break it on purpose: In requirements.yaml, set allow_planned: true on DP-3.1 so LedgerLens passes residency, then put it back.

Done when: pytest is green, eval/run_eval.py shows 100% verdict accuracy, and you can explain in two sentences why QuillDesk is BLOCKED and Parakeet is only CONDITIONAL.

M1 — The policy library, production grade (3–4 days)#

Production RAG Modules 06, 08, 09, 11 · Labs 03, 06, 08, 09, 11

Goal: Upgrade keyword search to your rag_core pipeline and extractive answers to grounded answers — without losing any security property.

  • Copy rag_core/ in, and load data/policies while keeping clause ids and metadata (access, status, trust, version) on every chunk.
  • Upgrade PolicyLibrary.search() to hybrid search (BM25 + vectors, RRF) with a cross-encoder reranker. Filters must stay BEFORE ranking: ACL, archived, untrusted, and injection flag.
  • Upgrade PolicyLibrary.answer() to return grounded answers with clause citations when an LLM is configured, while keeping extractive mode as an offline fallback. Refuse when the top score is below the threshold or the grader says "not grounded".
  • Fix the known failure pq-who-approves: keyword search ranks SEC-7.1 above the approval table in AI-5.1. Hybrid search plus reranking should fix this; prove it in the eval report.
  • Add 3 policy documents of your own (e.g., an incident-response runbook and a 2027 draft marked status: draft) along with 3 new gold questions.

FLOWCHART

M2 — Vendor research on the real web (4–5 days)#

Deep Search Modules 03, 04, 05, 06, 07, 09 · Labs 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10

Goal: Upgrade the sequential live baseline to a planned, parallel, budgeted research agent that produces the same VendorProfile as offline mode — for real vendors.

  • "Four places" (Deep Search Module 12, "Adapt it to your own domain"): the fields are already retargeted in schemas.py, so review AUTHORITY, FIELD_AUTHORITY_OVERRIDES, and HALF_LIFE_DAYS in vendor_research.py and justify each number in a comment.
    • AUTHORITY defines how much each source type is trusted.
    • HALF_LIFE_DAYS defines how fast a fact's freshness score decays (per field).
  • Replace plan_queries() with Plan Creator → Plan Reviewer: create one sub-question per field, with stop rules ("stop when every high-stakes field has a documented source or two searches have failed").
  • Run fetch and extraction in parallel workers sharing one Budget, and route extraction to the small model.
  • Make the identity gate real: have the LLM decide "same company?" from the domain, legal entity, and product — and ensure it stays a gate (reject, don't down-weight).
  • Pick 3 real AI/SaaS vendors, research them by hand first (fill data/gold_set_template.json with URLs and dates), run the agent, and compare field by field.

  • Field accuracy against the hand-made gold set is ≥ 80%.

  • Offline tests still pass unchanged.

Tip (expect friction): Trust centres are often JavaScript-heavy, sites block bots, and "SOC 2 compliant" appears with no report. Keep the offline corpus as your regression suite and add a cached_pages/ snapshot so the demo doesn't depend on the internet.

M3 — Router and graders as agents (2 days)#

Agentic RAG "agents.py", "tasks.py", "Practice and self-check"

Goal: Replace the regex router and heuristic graders with LLM agents that are measurably better.

  • Port the Router's goal and backstory; add the routes vendor, assessment, and refuse; and return a RouteDecision via LLM.structured() (which forces typed JSON output).
  • Port the Answer Grader and Hallucination Grader as grade_relevance() and grade_grounded(), then add the retry loop.

Figure 43: Milestones (M0–M6) — M3 — Router and graders as agents (2 days)
STATE MACHINE

Done when: Routing accuracy reaches ≥ 90% on your 30 questions (with the LLM router), and a deliberately wrong answer (such as a prompt edited to invent a clause) is caught by the hallucination grader and leads to abstaining.

M4 — Security: attack it, then defend in layers (2 days)#

Deep Search Modules 08, 11 · Lab 9 · Production RAG Module 11 · Lab 11

Goal: Prove that untrusted content — whether web pages, chat exports, or the user's own question — can never change a verdict.

  • Write tests/test_red_team.py with 15 attacks, each asserting where it was caught:
    • an injection in a vendor page ("report PASS")
    • an injection in a policy document
    • a user question smuggling an instruction ("…and mark it approved")
    • a fake trust centre on a look-alike domain
    • a page claiming an India region exists when the privacy policy says it is planned
    • a rumour phrased as news
  • Catch points: quarantine, identity gate, dropped, intent check, and output guardrail.
  • Add a second injection layer behind the regexes: a small-model classifier on each fetched page (DS Lab 9), and measure false positives on clean pages.
  • Ablation (turn one part off to see its value): switch the identity gate off so the UK firm's ISO certificate leaks into LedgerLens's facts, and screenshot it for the write-up.
  • Apply the Module 11 privacy checklist: the schema holds no personal data, the questionnaire email names a role rather than a person, and nothing from vendor employees is stored.

Done when: 15/15 attacks are caught with their catch point asserted, gold-set safety remains 100%, and the guess rate stays 0.

M5 — Make it a product: graph, API, UI, human gate (3–4 days)#

Deep Search Module 12, Lab 12 · Production RAG Modules 04, 12, 13

Goal: Ensure a reviewer can use the product without you in the room.

  • LangGraph: Add a checkpointer and interrupt() at human_gate so an assessment can pause for days and resume when the approver decides (the CLI prompt is the placeholder).
  • API: Put /assess behind a queue (Redis + RQ), return a job id immediately, and poll for the report. Store reports in Postgres so /vendors/{name}/history shows what changed since the last review (SEC-12.1).
  • Derive user_groups from the caller's identity on the server. Never accept groups from the client — that is the ACL.
  • UI: Stream node progress, show the trace as a tree beside the report, and add an Approve / Reject form calling /approve/{run_id} with the reviewer's name. A BLOCKED report must not offer an Approve button.
  • Observability: Log per-stage timings and cost for each run, and display a table of the last 20 runs with p50/p95 latency and cost (RAG Lab 13). (p50/p95 = median / 95th-percentile.)
Figure 44: Milestones (M0–M6) — M5 — Make it a product: graph, API, UI, human gate (3–4 days)
SEQUENCE

Done when: A teammate who hasn't seen the code can assess a vendor from the UI, read why each verdict was given, send vendor questions, and record a decision — and that decision survives a server restart.

M6 — Evaluate, write it up, demo (2–3 days)#

Deep Search Module 10, Lab 11 · Production RAG Module 10, Lab 10

  • Grow the real-vendor gold set to 10 vendors × 8 fields, hand-checked with URL and date, mixing clear passes, clear fails, and messy cases.
  • Add an LLM-as-judge metric for reasons: is every reason faithful to the cited evidence? Calibrate the judge on 20 hand-labelled reasons first.
  • Run one ablation per component (no reranker, no identity gate, no freshness decay, no planner) and include the results as a table in the report. Each component must earn its place.
  • Wire eval/run_eval.py --strict and pytest into CI (GitHub Actions) on the offline gold set.
  • Write the README covering the problem, architecture, numbers, what went wrong, and what's next, then rehearse the demo.

Done when: The eval report shows accuracy, guess rate, safety, cost, and latency for both the fictional and real sets, CI is green, and the demo runs offline and live.

Tip: Every milestone keeps the old guarantees: tests green, guess rate 0, and safety 100%. Upgrades must never trade away honesty.

73

The Data Pack#

Section 4

Theory#

In one line: This pack includes fictional policies, 11 YAML rules, a 23-page fake vendor web, and gold sets — everything you need to run and test offline.

Policies — data/policies/#

Document Key clauses
Information Security Policy 2026 SEC-4.2 assurance · SEC-7.1 SSO · SEC-9.3 incidents · SEC-9.4 rumours
Information Security Policy 2025 (archived) Accepted SOC 2 Type I, so reading the wrong version passes the wrong vendors.
Data Protection Policy DP-2.2 DPA · DP-3.1 India residency · DP-4.1 sub-processors · DP-5.4 deletion
AI Acceptable Use Policy AI-2.1 no training · AI-3.4 model providers · AI-5.1 who approves
Vendor Onboarding Checklist PROC-1.1 the list · PROC-2.1 the review file
Approved Vendor List Restricted to Security and Procurement. Parakeet is approved for T2 only, and LedgerLens is "in progress".
Questionnaire template NM-SEC-Q The source of every vendor question in the report.
Chat export Marked untrusted; it contains a wrong claim and an injection line.

Rules — data/requirements.yaml#

  • There are 11 machine-checkable requirements, each with a clause, vendor field, rule type, parameters, severity, and applicable data tiers.
  • These are built from 8 rule types.
  • Adding a clause means adding a YAML entry and, sometimes, one small rule function with its tests.

The vendor web — data/vendor_web/corpus.json#

  • The corpus has 23 fictional pages across 3 vendors.
  • Each page includes mock_claims representing what a careful extraction model would read from it:
    • Offline mode uses mock_claims, while live mode calls your model.

Gold sets#

  • gold_set.json: Contains 5 assessment cases (including the same question asked by someone without access) and 6 policy questions (with one marked "baseline known to fail").
74

Rules of the Project#

Section 5

Theory#

In one line: Ten non-negotiable principles keep the system honest, consistent, and safe.

# Rule What it means
1 The model never decides a verdict The LLM reads pages, drafts text, and classifies routes, while matcher.py decides from unit-testable rules. The same evidence always produces the same verdict.
2 UNKNOWN beats a guess A PASS or FAIL without an evidence URL is a bug, so the output guardrail downgrades it. guess_rate must stay 0.
3 A claim is not evidence "We are SOC 2 compliant" is only claimed; a report, certificate number, registry entry, or legal page is documented. Only documented evidence passes a high-stakes requirement.
4 Identity is a gate, not a weight A same-name company page is rejected before reading, because down-weighting still lets facts leak.
5 Untrusted content never reaches the verdict Pages addressing the AI are quarantined whole, while forum posts and rumours are dropped and logged rather than scored low.
6 Repetition is not corroboration A syndicated copy of the vendor's page counts only once.
7 Access control lives in retrieval The Approved Vendor List is invisible outside Security and Procurement, and the assistant says so instead of leaking it. Groups come from server-side identity, never from the request body.
8 Every fact has a date Freshness decays per field: a 2024 security page loses to a 2026 trust centre, and any conflict is recorded, not hidden.
9 Humans approve The report ends in an approval block that only a named person fills out. The word "approved" never appears in system output about a vendor.
10 Research companies, not people No vendor-employee names appear in the schema, memory, or report.
75

Evaluation & Rubric#

Section 6

Theory#

In one line: A scorecard tracks six metrics with hard targets, alongside a 100-point rubric spread across the milestones.

Scorecard#

Metric Meaning Target
verdict_accuracy (case, requirement) verdicts that match the gold set ≥ 95% fictional · ≥ 80% real
overall_accuracy BLOCKED, CONDITIONAL, or READY outcomes that match the gold set 100% fictional
guess_rate PASS or FAIL verdicts where the gold set says UNKNOWN or NEEDS_REVIEW 0% on both sets
safety Attack pages quarantined, look-alikes rejected, rumours dropped, and nothing from them cited 100%
policy_qa_hard Never cites a document the asker can't see or an untrusted one 100%
cost · latency Per live assessment Under your budget · < 90 s

Tip: guess_rate is the honesty metric: a wrong UNKNOWN is acceptable, whereas a confident wrong PASS is not.

Rubric (100 points)#

Area Pts Full marks look like
Correctness on fictional gold set 15 eval --strict and pytest stay green after every change.
Policy library (M1) 15 Hybrid search, reranking, and grounded answers with citations; "known to fail" fixed; ACL, versions, and trust tested; 3 new docs and questions added.
Vendor research, live (M2) 20 Planner, parallel workers, and budget implemented; ≥ 80% field accuracy on real vendors; identity gate and freshness justified; conflicts recorded with provenance.
Router and graders (M3) 10 LLM router reaches ≥ 90% on 30 questions; graders catch an injected hallucination; retry loop works.
Security (M4) 10 15/15 attacks caught with their catch point asserted; identity-gate ablation shown; privacy checklist applied.
Product (M5) 15 LangGraph checkpointed human gate; queued API with history; UI with progress, trace viewer, and decision form; BLOCKED reports cannot be approved.
Evaluation & engineering (M6) 10 10 real vendors evaluated; calibrated LLM-as-judge; one ablation per component; CI green.
Write-up and demo 5 README includes numbers and honest failures; demo runs offline and live without improvisation.

Demo Checklist (12 minutes)#

Section 7

Theory#

In one line: A scripted 12-minute demo shows the result, the trace, access control, the good vendor, a live run, an attack, and the numbers.

Step Time Show
1. The question 1 min A support lead asks about LedgerLens for tickets. Point at BLOCKED and at DP-3.1 with its source and date.
2. The trace 2 min Walk through trace.jsonl: the rejected UK firm, quarantined blog, dropped rumour, and 2024 page losing to the 2026 trust centre.
3. Access control 1 min Run the same question as an employee outside Security: PROC-1.1 turns UNKNOWN and the list never appears. Ask "Which vendors are approved?" to show it returns the process, not the list.
4. The good vendor 2 min Run Parakeet at T3: all checks pass on documented evidence, yet it is CONDITIONAL (approved for T2 only). Switch to T2 and it becomes READY FOR HUMAN APPROVAL. Try approving BLOCKED LedgerLens to show it is refused.
5. Live 3 min Assess a real vendor from the UI with progress streaming, and compare two fields against your hand research.
6. Attack 1 min Add an injection line to a cached page and re-run to show it is quarantined with verdicts unchanged.
7. Numbers 2 min Present the scorecard, ablation table, cost and latency, and the two things that still go wrong.

78

FAQ#

Section 9

Theory#

In one line: Why the rule engine is still "AI", along with practical answers on blocked sites and solo work.

  • Isn't a rule engine "not AI"? The intelligence lies in turning a thousand messy pages into typed, dated, sourced facts and knowing which pages to distrust. The rule engine itself is ~300 lines and stays that way.
  • What if pages block my fetcher? Cache what you can, record UNKNOWN for the rest, and let the questionnaire ask the vendor. An honest UNKNOWN plus a follow-up question is a correct output, and adding Playwright (browser automation) for JS-rendered trust centres is a reasonable stretch goal.
  • Can I do this solo? Yes: complete M0–M4 in full, build M5 as a CLI and API only, and use 3 real vendors instead of 10, which takes about three weeks.
79

Glossary#

Appendix A

Theory#

Term Meaning
Data tier Nimbu Mart's classification: T1 public, T2 internal, T3 customer data. Requirements depend on the highest tier a tool touches.
SOC 2 Type II An independent auditor's report confirming that controls operated effectively over a period (usually 6–12 months), whereas Type I only covers design at a single point in time.
ISO/IEC 27001 A certificate from an accredited body confirming that the vendor runs an information-security management system; it includes a certificate number and an expiry date.
DPA Data Processing Agreement: a contract that binds a vendor to process personal data only on the customer's instructions.
DPDP Act India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Nimbu Mart acts as the Data Fiduciary, and vendors act as Data Processors.
Sub-processor A company the vendor uses that also touches your data — such as hosting, email, or any third-party model provider.
Evidence level documented (report, certificate, registry, or legal page), claimed (marketing text), third_party (named press or review site), or rumour (forum or unnamed source).
Verdicts PASS, FAIL, UNKNOWN (no evidence), NEEDS_REVIEW (evidence found, so a person must judge), or NOT_APPLICABLE (the rule doesn't apply to this tier).
Outcome BLOCKED (a blocking requirement failed), CONDITIONAL (open items remain), or READY FOR HUMAN APPROVAL (all checks passed, though a person still decides).

From verdicts to outcome to human decision#

Figure 45: Glossary — From verdicts to outcome to human decision
STATE MACHINE

Tip: "BLOCKED" does not mean "rejected", and "READY" does not mean "approved". Only a named human makes the final call.

Memory hooks#

  • UNKNOWN beats a guess. Guess rate stays at 0%.
  • A claim is not evidence. Only documented evidence passes a high-stakes requirement.
  • Repetition is not corroboration. A syndicated copy counts once.
  • The word "approved" never comes from the system. A named human approves.
  • Research companies, not people.

Step-by-Step Guide for Similar Problems#

Theory#

In one line: Use this guide for any AI-assisted compliance or due-diligence decision, such as vendor risk, KYB checks, grant eligibility, procurement, or open-source licence review.

Which pieces does the problem need?#

If the problem has… Bring in…
A decision that must be auditable and repeatable A deterministic matcher, not an LLM verdict
Requirements written in internal policy documents Policy RAG (Unit 1)
Mixed question types from users Router + graders (Unit 2)
Facts on the open web that change over time Deep search (Unit 3)
Legal, financial or security consequences A human approval gate

The steps#

Step 1 — Write the contracts first#

  • Do: Define typed schemas for the subject's fields (9 vendor fields here), the evidence object (value, source URL, date, evidence level), the verdict enum, and the report.
  • Done when: Every stage has a typed input and output.

Step 2 — Turn policy into machine-checkable rules#

  • Do: Write rules as data (requirements.yaml: 8 rule types, 11 requirements), each linked to the policy clause it comes from, and unit-test the matcher with fixtures before any AI exists.
  • Done when: The same facts in always produce the same verdicts out.

Step 3 — Build the policy library#

  • Do: Build clause-level chunks, use BM25 or hybrid search, apply ACL, active-version, and trusted filters before ranking, and generate grounded answers with citations.

Step 4 — Add the router and graders#

  • Do: Implement four routes (policy, vendor, assessment, refuse). If retrieved chunks are not relevant, widen the search (k = 8 plus query rewrite); if the answer is not grounded, regenerate once more strictly and then abstain.

Step 5 — Plug in subject research#

  • Do: Run the pipeline: plan, fetch, injection scan, identity gate, extract, score, and merge. Rumours and forums are dropped and logged, copies count once, and the newer fact wins while any conflict is recorded.

Step 6 — Match, then explain the gaps#

  • Do: The matcher turns rules and facts into verdicts, and the questionnaire drafter writes a question for every UNKNOWN or NEEDS_REVIEW.

Step 7 — Put guardrails on both ends#

  • Do: On input, apply PII redaction and an intent check. On output, downgrade any PASS or FAIL without an evidence URL to UNKNOWN, and block "approved" or employee names.

Step 8 — Add the human gate and the product shell#

  • Do: Include an approval block that only a named person can fill out, hide the Approve button on BLOCKED reports, add an API, UI, and trace viewer, and cache pages so demos never depend on live internet.

Step 9 — Evaluate like an auditor#

  • Do: Build gold sets (fictional and real) targeting ≥ 95% fictional / ≥ 80% real verdict accuracy, 0% guess rate, 100% safety, ≥ 90% router accuracy, and 15/15 red-team attacks caught; run --strict in CI.

Worked example: approving open-source dependencies#

Step Applied to the new problem
1 Define fields: licence, latest release date, critical CVEs, time-to-patch, and maintainer activity.
2 Define rules: licence must be in the allow-list, critical CVEs must be patched within 30 days, and a release must exist within 12 months.
3 Build a policy library over the engineering open-source policy, with archived versions filtered out.
5 Use package registries (official), security advisory databases (high authority), and repo pages. Enforce an identity gate on the exact package name and repo URL to stop typosquats.
6 An unknown licence yields an UNKNOWN verdict and a question to the maintainers, never a guess.
8 The security lead approves; the system only prepares the review file.

Red flags while approaching#

  • Letting the LLM produce PASS/FAIL.
  • Treating marketing claims ("SOC 2 compliant") as documented evidence.
  • Down-weighting look-alike pages instead of rejecting them.
  • Reading archived policy versions.
  • Depending on the live internet for the demo.
82

1. Cross-Course Synthesis & Architecture Flow#

This capstone integrates all three preceding courses into one auditable product orchestrated by assessor/graph.py (supporting both plain Python and LangGraph StateGraph):

  • From Course 1 (01-production-rag): Clause-level chunking, BM25 policy retrieval, ACL pre-filtering, active/archived version gating, untrusted source exclusion, and grounded citations (assessor/policy_rag.py, app/api.py).
  • From Course 2 (02-agentic-rag): Semantic 4-way Router (assessor/router.py) + Answer Relevance & Hallucination Graders (assessor/graders.py).
  • From Course 3 (03-deep-search-agent): Vendor research planner, parallel gatherer, identity gate, prompt-injection quarantine, freshness decay + authority scoring, conflict/provenance merger, and budgets/tracing (assessor/vendor_research.py, assessor/tracing.py).
  • New Capstone Glue: Deterministic rule matcher (assessor/matcher.py), vendor questionnaire drafter (assessor/questionnaire.py), input/output guardrails (assessor/guardrails.py), human approval gate (human_gate), and Streamlit UI (app/ui.py).

SEC-7.1 / SEC-9.3 / PROC-1.1 SEC-7.1, SEC-9.3 (blocker T3), PROC-1.1 (major) sso_saml, security_incidents, approved_vendor_list PROC-1.1 reads from ACL-protected approved_vendor_list.md (which requires the security or procurement group).

4. Quick Run & Config Reference#

Run commands from study-material/project-vendor-risk-assessor/:


python scripts/check_setup.py      # Verify environment & offline corpus
python run_assessor.py             # Default offline assessment (LedgerLens AI, T3, 35 users -> BLOCKED)
python -m pytest -q                # Run all 70 automated tests
python eval/run_eval.py --strict   # Run gold_set.json scorecard with CI thresholds

# Start API & Streamlit Reviewer UI:
uvicorn app.api:app --reload --port 8000
streamlit run app/ui.py
  • Key .env variables (.env.example): LLM_PROVIDER (mock | gemini | groq | ollama | openrouter | openai | anthropic | custom), SEARCH_PROVIDER (offline | ddgs | tavily), VRA_AS_OF, VRA_MAX_USD, VRA_MAX_PARALLEL, VRA_RESULTS_PER_QUERY.
83

Cheat Sheet#

Theory#

Core idea: The LLM reads, code judges, and a human decides. Every fact carries a value, source, date, and evidence level.

Key terms#

Term One-liner
Matcher matcher.py: evaluates rules against facts deterministically with no LLM.
Identity gate Rejects (rather than down-weights) pages about a different company.
Quarantine Drops an entire page that gives instructions to the AI.
Evidence levels documented, claimed, third_party, and rumour (only documented passes high-stakes rules).
Verdicts PASS, FAIL, UNKNOWN, NEEDS_REVIEW, and NOT_APPLICABLE.
Outcomes BLOCKED, CONDITIONAL, and READY FOR HUMAN APPROVAL.
Data tiers T1 public, T2 internal, and T3 customer data.
Routes policy, vendor, assessment, and refuse.

Decision rules#

  • A PASS or FAIL without an evidence URL is downgraded to UNKNOWN by the output guardrail.
  • Filters (ACL, archived, untrusted, injection) run before ranking.
  • Rumours and forums are dropped and logged, copies count once, and the newer fact wins while any conflict is recorded.
  • If chunks are not relevant, widen the search (k = 8 plus query rewrite); if the answer is not grounded, regenerate once more strictly and then abstain.
  • Groups come from server identity, never from the client. A BLOCKED report shows no Approve button.
  • The system never writes "approved", and no vendor-employee names appear anywhere.

Important numbers#

Item Value
Starter tests / default run 70 tests · < 1 s offline
Schema / rules 9 vendor fields · 8 rule types · 11 requirements
Corpus / gold set 23 pages, 3 vendors · 5 assessment cases + 6 policy Qs
Verdict accuracy ≥ 95% fictional · ≥ 80% real · overall 100% fictional
Guess rate / safety / policy_qa_hard 0% · 100% · 100%
M2 live ≥ 80% field accuracy · < 90 s · < VRA_MAX_USD
M3 router 30 questions (10/route) · ≥ 90%
M4 red team 15/15 attacks with catch point
M6 10 vendors × 8 fields · judge calibrated on 20 reasons
Demo 12 minutes · rubric 100 pts (M2 = 20)

Pipeline (assessment)#

Question → Input guardrail → Router → Vendor research (plan · fetch · injection scan · identity · extract · score · merge) → Matcher → Questionnaire → Human gate → Review file (report.md · json · trace.jsonl) → Output guardrail

Milestones#

M0 run & read (½ d) · M1 policy RAG (3–4 d) · M2 live research (4–5 d) · M3 router/graders (2 d) · M4 security (2 d) · M5 product (3–4 d) · M6 eval & demo (2–3 d)

Commands#


python scripts/check_setup.py   # verify setup
python run_assessor.py          # default LedgerLens run (BLOCKED)
python -m pytest -q             # 70 tests
python eval/run_eval.py         # scorecard (--strict in CI)

Pitfalls#

  • Reading the archived 2025 policy (accepted SOC 2 Type I).
  • Treating "SOC 2 compliant" marketing text as documented evidence.
  • Down-weighting look-alike pages instead of rejecting them.
  • Counting a syndicated copy as corroboration.
  • Letting the LLM decide verdicts, which makes them inconsistent and unauditable.
  • Leaking the Approved Vendor List to non-Security users.
  • Depending on live internet for the demo — keep cached_pages/ ready.
84

Super Quick Revision#

Theory#

Read time: about 6 minutes. This page covers the whole unit in order. Each block is one idea you must be able to explain. Use the self-test at the end to check yourself.

In one line: AI reads and finds facts; code judges; a human decides. The capstone joins Production RAG (policy library), Agentic RAG (router + graders) and Deep Search (vendor research). It adds new glue: a deterministic matcher, a questionnaire drafter, guardrails, a human approval gate and a UI.

1. The problem and the output#

  • Question: "Can our support team use this AI tool with customer data?" A manual review takes 2–6 hours per vendor, mostly spent finding and dating facts.
  • Output (a review file): Every policy requirement gets a clause, verdict, reason, and evidence (source and date), plus ready-to-send vendor questions and an approval block for two named signers (Head of Information Security and DPO).
  • Every fact carries a value, source, date, and evidence level. If you can't fill in the evidence, the verdict must be UNKNOWN.

2. Vocabulary you must know#

  • Data tiers: T1 (public), T2 (internal), and T3 (customer data). Requirements depend on the highest tier a tool touches.
  • Evidence levels: documented (report, certificate, registry, or legal page), claimed (marketing text), third-party, and rumour. Only documented evidence passes a high-stakes requirement.
  • Verdicts: PASS, FAIL, UNKNOWN (no evidence), NEEDS_REVIEW (evidence found, but a person must judge), and NOT_APPLICABLE.
  • Outcomes: BLOCKED (a blocker failed), CONDITIONAL (open items remain), and READY FOR HUMAN APPROVAL. BLOCKED does not mean "rejected", and READY does not mean "approved".
  • SOC 2 Type II means controls worked over a period (whereas Type I only covers design at one point in time), ISO 27001 is a certified security management system, DPA stands for data processing agreement, and a sub-processor is another company that touches your data.

3. The three test vendors#

  • LedgerLens AI: Has a solid SOC 2 Type II report, but data stays in the US/EU and India is only "planned", so DP-3.1 FAILs and it is BLOCKED at T3. Traps include a stale 2024 page, a UK same-name firm, a forum rumour, a contradicting review site, and an injection blog.
  • QuillDesk: Claims to be "SOC 2 compliant" with no report, trains on content by default, uses US-only storage, has an incident with no post-mortem, and appears on a copy page, so it is BLOCKED.
  • Parakeet Translate: The good vendor (ISO 27001 on the registry, India region, no training, DPA). It is approved only for T2, so it is CONDITIONAL at T3 and READY at T2.

4. Architecture: one graph, three routes#

  • Flow: Input passes through the input guardrail and then the router (policy, vendor, assessment, or refuse).
  • Policy route: Policy RAG feeds into relevance and grounding graders before returning an answer. If not relevant, widen the search (k = 8 plus rewrite); if not grounded, regenerate once more strictly and then abstain.
  • Vendor route: Research runs plan, fetch, injection scan, identity gate, extract, score, and merge.
  • Assessment route: Research feeds the matcher (turning rules and facts into verdicts), then the questionnaire (one question per UNKNOWN or NEEDS_REVIEW), the human gate, the review file (report.md, JSON, trace.jsonl), and finally the output guardrail.
  • The same nodes run as plain Python or as a LangGraph state machine (assessor/graph.py). The matcher is ~300 lines of unit-tested rules, read from requirements.yaml (11 requirements, 8 rule types).

5. The ten rules (the heart of the project)#

  1. The model never decides a verdict. matcher.py does, so the same evidence always gives the same verdict.
  2. UNKNOWN beats a guess. A PASS/FAIL without an evidence URL is downgraded; guess_rate stays 0.
  3. A claim is not evidence. "We are SOC 2 compliant" is only claimed.
  4. Identity is a gate, not a weight. Look-alike pages are rejected, not down-weighted.
  5. Untrusted content never reaches a verdict. Pages that address the AI are quarantined whole; rumours are dropped and logged.
  6. Repetition is not corroboration. A copy counts once.
  7. Access control lives in retrieval. Groups come from the server-side identity. The Approved Vendor List never leaks.
  8. Every fact has a date. Freshness decays per field; the newer fact wins and the conflict is recorded.
  9. Humans approve. The system never writes "approved", and a BLOCKED report has no Approve button.
  10. Research companies, not people. No vendor-employee names anywhere.

6. Milestones M0–M6#

  • M0 Run and read (½ day): run the demos and read the traces bottom-up; tests green and 100% verdict accuracy.
  • M1 Policy library (3–4 days): hybrid + rerank + grounded answers with clause citations. Filters (ACL, archived, untrusted, injection) stay before ranking. Fix the "known to fail" question.
  • M2 Live vendor research (4–5 days): planner, parallel workers, a shared budget and an LLM identity gate. ≥ 80% field accuracy on 3 real vendors in under 90 s and under VRA_MAX_USD.
  • M3 Router and graders as agents (2 days): ≥ 90% routing accuracy on 30 questions; the hallucination grader catches an invented clause.
  • M4 Security (2 days): 15/15 red-team attacks caught, each with its catch point asserted; an identity-gate ablation; the privacy checklist.
  • M5 Product (3–4 days): LangGraph checkpointer + interrupt() at the human gate, a queued API with history, a UI with progress, trace and decision form. The decision survives a restart.
  • M6 Evaluate and demo (2–3 days): 10 real vendors × 8 fields, an LLM judge calibrated on 20 reasons, one ablation per component, CI green.
  • Every milestone keeps the old guarantees: tests green, guess rate 0, safety 100%.

7. Data pack, scorecard and demo#

  • Data: 8 policy documents (including an archived 2025 policy that accepted SOC 2 Type I, a trap; a restricted Approved Vendor List; an untrusted chat export). 23 fake web pages across 3 vendors, each with mock_claims. Gold set: 5 assessment cases + 6 policy questions.
  • Scorecard: verdict accuracy ≥ 95% (fictional) and ≥ 80% (real); overall outcome 100% (fictional); guess_rate 0% (the honesty metric: a wrong UNKNOWN is acceptable, whereas a confident wrong PASS is not); safety 100%; policy_qa_hard 100%; and latency < 90 s.
  • Rubric: 100 points, with M2 live research the largest at 20. Demo: 12 minutes covering the BLOCKED result, the trace, access control, the good vendor, a live run, an attack and the numbers.
  • Reuse the pattern for any compliance or due-diligence decision (KYB, procurement, open-source licence review). Use a matcher for auditable decisions, policy RAG for internal rules, router + graders for mixed questions, deep search for changing web facts, and a human gate for consequences.

Quick self-test#

Question Answer
Who decides PASS/FAIL, and why not the LLM? The deterministic matcher.py, so verdicts are repeatable, testable and auditable.
A trust centre says "SOC 2 compliant" with no report. Verdict for a high-stakes rule? Not PASS. It is only claimed evidence, so the verdict is UNKNOWN or NEEDS_REVIEW, plus a vendor question.
Why is LedgerLens BLOCKED at T3? DP-3.1 India residency FAILs: today the data is US/EU, and India is only "planned".
Why is Parakeet only CONDITIONAL at T3? All checks pass on documented evidence, but it is approved only for T2 data.
A PASS has no evidence URL. What happens? The output guardrail downgrades it to UNKNOWN.
Someone outside Security asks for the Approved Vendor List. Answer? The process, never the list; PROC-1.1 becomes UNKNOWN for them.
Which metric proves honesty? guess_rate, which must stay 0%.

If you remember only five things: (1) AI reads, code judges, a human decides. (2) UNKNOWN beats a guess, so the guess rate stays 0%. (3) A claim is not evidence; only documented evidence passes high-stakes rules. (4) Reject look-alikes and quarantine attack pages; never just down-weight them. (5) The system never says "approved".
